title: How Adobe Firefly took Real Madrid to the Moon
summary: Adobe details how Firefly was utilized in campaigns to bring Real Madrid to the Moon
detailed: Adobe partnered with Real Madrid to create a promotional video featuring six players from the men's and women's teams wearing an unreleased Adidas kit.
The production team faced a tight timeline of under a month from storyboard to edit, with a strict 45-minute window to photograph the players on set.
The project utilized Adobe Firefly and the Kling partner model to generate supernatural elements like lunar surfaces, clouds, and flying wings based on reference photographs.
Real Madrid provided strict oversight during post-production to protect valuable intellectual property, including player likenesses, the club crest, and the new kit.
sentences: Adobe campaign briefs are often ambitious, but this one was out of this world.
For a collaboration between Adobe Firefly and Real Madrid, creative director Jan Gensch and director Joffrey Jans developed a story told through the imagination of a young football supporter.

It would begin in her family’s living room, then follow Real Madrid players as they sprinted through clouds, rose alongside flying whales, and traveled through space to kick a flaming football on the moon.
Adobe has partnered with Real Madrid on digital fan experiences since 2021, and this new campaign would involve some of the club’s most protected assets.
Six professional men’s and women’s team players were available to star in the film, wearing a new-season Adidas kit that was still under wraps.
In every frame, we had to preserve Real Madrid’s valuable intellectual property, from the famous club crest and white football kit, to the players’ likenesses.
Real Madrid needed to time the release of the video to the new kit launch and the start of Spain’s La Liga football season.
That gave us less than a month to go from storyboard to shoot and edit.
Then, we found out we only had 45 minutes with the players.
We decided to build a photography studio to capture each player's likeness accurately, then use those stills to build the fantasy in Adobe Firefly, our AI creative studio.
We started in Firefly Boards, where Adobe, Real Madrid, and the production team worked on one shared canvas.
Instead of creating presentations and waiting for feedback, we all collaborated live on visual directions.
In a matter of days, we had turned animated stills into a moving prototype of Real Madrid players flying through space with futuristic wings.
The club could react to early ideas and see how its crest, kit, and players would be represented while there was still time to change course.
The prototype was so convincing that our Real Madrid colleagues treated it like a finished film.
That decision told the production team which player photographs, poses, and angles it needed to capture when the clock started on set.
Our film crew joined the team at the player shoot in Madrid.
I’m from Spain and support Sevilla FC, but I call Real Madrid my “spiritual team,” so it’s always a thrill to work with them.
Our production team had built an entire photographic studio to capture the players from several angles, along with still life images of the new kit and match ball.
We were some of the first people on Earth to see the new jersey with its green collar and pink Adidas stripes.
Soon the players arrived, ready for action: Linda Caicedo, Maëlle Lakrar, and Sara Däbritz from the women’s team, and Dean Huijsen, Arda Güler, and Federico “Fede” Valverde from the men’s team.
Players are used to performing in sponsor shoots where they hold up a product and say a line.
Even though they had seen our interplanetary ideas on storyboards, we told them there would be no green screens, motion capture suits, or dangerous stunts.
After all, these are elite athletes, not actors.
Our photographers simply asked them to hold a series of poses so we could capture their likenesses.
We had to get what we needed fast; there would be no overtime.
The designers brought those photographs into Firefly as references, along with images of the new Adidas kit and match ball.
Our AI artists drew on deep knowledge of composition, color, and creative standards to write prompts that produced accurate player images, then refined each shot against the reference photograph.
The team used Kling, a partner model available in Firefly, to develop cloudscapes, metallic wings, the lunar surface, and other supernatural elements.
A separate live-action shoot captured the girl and the fans.
With those scenes filmed, the editors could bring the two worlds together.
Our team was entrusted with some of the most valuable intellectual property in the history of football.
Real Madrid’s players have worn the club’s famous crest to a record 15 European Cup victories, and the new Adidas match ball features complex patterns designed to deter counterfeiters.
During post-production, the club gave us detailed feedback on the kit, ball, player likenesses, and movement for errors and inconsistencies.
For pixel perfection some of the assets were finished in Adobe Photoshop.
Like any football match, there was drama right until the final minute.
One cloud-running sequence ended a second or two before the editors needed it to.
A reshoot was out of the question, so we used Firefly inside Adobe Premiere Pro to extend the film with extra frames.
For all the technology used to create this futuristic film, the finished edit begins with "Cómo no te voy a querer", a chant Real Madrid supporters have sung around the world for years.
The title means “How could I not love you?” and our team recorded it with a real choir.
We used that familiar song to carry the film from the family living room into the girl's imagination.
The film begins with the girl watching a Real Madrid match with her family on television.
Then the players break through the clouds, flap metallic wings, float beside flying whales, and finally kick a flaming football across the moon.
The fantasy ends back in the living room, with the family embracing as the chant continues.
The result is a warm, imaginative film that combines Real Madrid’s history with creative technology that gives fans new ways to connect with the club.
Real Madrid unveiled the kit on June 3, and "FourFourTwo" called it “a beauty.” On August 22, the men’s team opened their league season with a 2–1 win at Espanyol.
And six days later, we released the film.
The campaign also showed how Firefly can turn a single photo session into a flexible production system.
The team used written prompts to generate astonishing footage while protecting Real Madrid’s valued brand assets.
We also added missing seconds in Premiere Pro without a reshoot, and carried the same visual world into a campaign of static banners, secondary films, and short social videos.
